title: Anselm's argument
hook: God is that than which nothing greater can be thought

segments.voice: Yesterday, John of Damascus and the icons: the maker of matter became matter. Your line was matter is not evil. What ordinary thing did you handle with care? Day one thousand two hundred forty-eight.

A monk is stuck. By his own account, he's been hunting for one single argument, short and complete, that would show God exists. It keeps slipping away. He tries to give up on it, and it won't leave him alone. Then one day it arrives, and he writes it down. His name is Anselm, and the surprising thing is where he puts the argument. Not in a lecture. In a prayer. The little book opens with Anselm talking to God, asking to see God's face. Only then, in the middle of praying, does he make his move.

Before the argument, Anselm gives his reason for making it. He says, in words close to these: I don't seek to understand so that I can believe. I believe so that I can understand. Faith, looking for understanding. Then he turns to a verse from the Psalms: "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God." And he starts with a definition. God is something than which nothing greater can be thought. Even the fool, he says, understands those words. So the idea is at least in his mind. Now Anselm uses a painter. Before painting, the painter has the picture in mind. After painting, it exists in the mind and on the wall. Which is greater? The one that's real too. So if that-than-which-nothing-greater-can-be-thought existed only in the mind, you could think of something greater: the same thing, but real. And that can't be. So, Anselm concludes, it must exist in reality. Not everyone was convinced. A monk named Gaunilo wrote a reply on behalf of the fool. Picture an island more perfect than any other, he said. Does that make it real? Anselm answered him, and the debate is still going among philosophers. But there's one more turn, and it's where today's line comes from. A few chapters later, Anselm says that God is not only that than which nothing greater can be thought. God is greater than can be thought. For Anselm, the argument isn't a fence around God. It ends at an edge, with more past it than the mind can hold.

Here's the practice: think the greatest thing you can. Settle, and breathe. Let your mind reach for the biggest, best thing it can hold. Mountains, oceans, a love that never fails, the whole night sky. Make it as great as you can. Then notice: whatever you've got, you can still think of something greater. Anselm said God is beyond even that reaching. Rest there, at the edge of your thinking. If you pray, you can turn toward God the way Anselm did, talking first. The bell holds the time.
Anselm's argument. God is that than which nothing greater can be thought, and, Anselm adds, greater than can be thought at all, an argument made inside a prayer.

Your line: greater than can be thought. Today, when you hit the edge of what you understand, at work, in a hard conversation, in prayer, let it be an edge, not a wall. Day one thousand two hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Christians meet Anselm's argument in philosophy and theology classes, where it is still argued for and against; some also read his Proslogion as a book of prayer.

fork.setup: you're Anselm. Gaunilo says: by your logic, a perfect island would have to exist. what do you do?
options: write an answer and keep the argument.
fork.reveal: Anselm wrote a reply to Gaunilo and kept his argument. the debate is still going among philosophers.

original.script: aliquid quo nihil maius cogitari possit
original.say: AH-lee-kwid kwoh NEE-hil MY-yoos koh-gee-TAH-ree POS-sit
original.note: Latin: something than which nothing greater can be thought, Anselm's definition of God in the Proslogion.

trapdoor: what you thought: a proof of God is a cold piece of logic.
what it means: Anselm's argument begins in prayer: if God is that than which nothing greater can be thought, God can't exist only in the mind.
what a scholar hears: Proslogion 15, where the definition flips: God is greater than can be thought, so the argument opens onto mystery.
recall: the Latin word for this love

notes: Anselm is paraphrased throughout (Deane's 1903 translation is not on the validator's list). Check: the search for a single argument (preface); the opening prayer and 'I believe in order to understand' (ch. 1); the definition, the fool, and the painter (ch. 2); 'greater than can be thought' (ch. 15).
The hook paraphrases the preface (he sought a single argument, nearly gave up, and the thought would not leave him); confirm.
'The debate is still going among philosophers' is general; confirm acceptable.
'Faith seeking understanding' was Anselm's original title for the Proslogion (Fides quaerens intellectum); not stated in the script, only used as a screen head.

Editor pass: the teach's last line now frames the claim as Anselm's ('For Anselm, ...') rather than the narrator's, and trades the door image (day 1232's theme) for the edge image the carry uses. Gaunilo's island rephrased closer to his 'more excellent than all other lands'.
Original: 'aliquid quo nihil maius cogitari possit' from Proslogion 2; ecclesiastical pronunciation would differ (MAH-yoos, koh-jee-TAH-ree).
